chapter_summary: Proverbs 17 is a richly concentrated collection of wisdom sayings covering the inner life of the heart, the power of words, the nature of true friendship, and the marks of wisdom versus folly. It shows that peace in a home is worth more than material abundance, that God Himself tests and knows the heart, that a wise person welcomes correction while a fool cannot, and that real friendship holds steady through every hard season. The chapter repeatedly contrasts the fool — who mocks the poor, stirs up trouble, and cannot hold his tongue — with the wise person who is slow to speak, quick to listen, and steady in spirit. Running through every verse is the conviction that God sees and responds to what is in the heart, not merely what is outwardly performed.
main_lesson: God cares about what is in your heart, not just what you do on the outside. A wise person is slow to speak, quick to forgive, and stays kind even when it is hard.

memory_verse.kjv: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
memory_verse.little_bible: A true friend loves you always. A brother is made for hard times.

parent_guide:
Proverbs 17 touches some of the most practically urgent themes in a child's daily life: conflict in the home, friendship that holds under pressure, the power of words to build or destroy, and the inner attitude of the heart before God. Verse 1 — the chapter's opening — sets the tone immediately: a peaceful home with little is better than a home full of abundance but racked with fighting. This is a profound statement for children to absorb, because it reorients value away from things and toward relationships.

Verse 3 is theologically foundational: God tests hearts the way a refiner tests silver and gold in fire. This means that difficulties in life are not random — God is at work in them, shaping character and revealing what is truly inside us. Children can understand this: 'When things are hard, God is helping you grow stronger and better.' Verse 10 teaches that wise people genuinely receive correction — a single word lands deeper than a hundred blows on a fool. This is a powerful conversation to have with children about how they receive correction at home and school.

Verses 14 and 27–28 bookend an important set of teachings about words. Starting an argument is like opening a crack in a dam — it is much easier to stop before it begins than after it has started. The wise person is one of few words; even a fool is thought wise when silent. These are concrete, memorable principles children can apply today.

For parents: use verse 17 ('A friend loveth at all times') as an anchor for conversations about what real friendship looks like versus fair-weather companions. Use verse 22 ('A merry heart doeth good like a medicine') to talk about joy, attitude, and the real difference a grateful spirit makes. And use verse 5 ('Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker') to teach the absolute dignity of every person God has made.
application_for_children: This week, practise being slow to speak and quick to listen. When you feel like arguing, stop before the first word. Ask God to put a kind heart and a quiet tongue inside you.

verses.kjv: Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife.
verses.little_bible: A peaceful home with little food is better. A home full of food but full of fighting is worse. Peace matters more than plenty.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A quiet, peaceful home is better than a fighting one.
verses.meaning: A small and simple meal eaten in peace is of greater value than a lavish feast consumed in the atmosphere of conflict and strife. 'Sacrifices' here refers to the festive meals that accompanied temple offerings — abundant and celebratory by nature. The point is that relational peace cannot be replaced by material abundance. Harmony in the home is a gift more precious than prosperity.
verses.prayer: God, make our home full of peace.
verses.discussion_question: Why is a peaceful home better than a rich one?
verses.family_discussion: What habits or patterns in our home create strife — and what would it look like to lay those down for the sake of peace? What is peace worth sacrificing for?
verses.do_it_today: Do one thing today to make your home more peaceful — speak kindly, say sorry, or stay quiet when you feel like arguing.
verses.illustration_prompt: A family happily sharing a small simple meal together at a plain table, warm golden light, gentle smiles, peaceful home, soft watercolour style

verses.kjv: A wise servant shall have rule over a son that causeth shame, and shall have part of the inheritance among the brethren.
verses.little_bible: A wise servant is worth more than a shameful son. Hard work and wisdom matter more than your family name.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A wise, hard worker is worth more than a foolish family member.
verses.meaning: In the ancient world, inheritance was reserved for biological sons. This proverb radically overturns that assumption: a servant who acts wisely will be trusted with authority even over the master's own son who brings shame. Character and wisdom outweigh birth position. God also rewards faithfulness regardless of one's starting place in life.
verses.prayer: God, help me be wise and faithful always.
verses.discussion_question: Why does wisdom matter more than who you are born to?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children understand that their character — not their birth, wealth, or position — is what truly determines their worth and their future?
verses.do_it_today: Do your chores or schoolwork today with your whole heart, as if it really matters — because it does.
verses.illustration_prompt: A diligent servant child working faithfully alongside a trusted elder, warm tones of honour and respect, soft watercolour scene

verses.kjv: The fining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the LORD trieth the hearts.
verses.little_bible: Fire tests silver and gold to make them pure. God tests our hearts to know what is truly inside us.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: God tests our hearts the way fire tests gold.
verses.meaning: Just as a refiner uses extreme heat to separate pure metal from impurities, God uses the trials and pressures of life to reveal and refine the true condition of the human heart. God does not need to test to gain knowledge — He already knows all. Rather, the testing reveals what is there, both to others and to ourselves. Nothing is hidden from God's sight.
verses.prayer: God, make my heart pure like refined gold.
verses.discussion_question: What does it mean that God tests our hearts?
verses.family_discussion: When our family faces difficulty, how do we frame that for our children — as something random and bad, or as something God is using to shape us? What would change if we consistently chose the second view?
verses.do_it_today: When something hard happens today, say out loud: 'God sees my heart. I choose to trust Him.'
verses.illustration_prompt: A goldsmith holding a glowing crucible over a flame, pure gold emerging, God's watchful presence as light over the scene, rich watercolour tones

verses.kjv: A wicked doer giveth heed to false lips; and a liar giveth ear to a naughty tongue.
verses.little_bible: A wicked person loves to hear lies. A liar enjoys hearing bad things about others. Wrong people enjoy wrong words.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Bad people love to hear lies and bad words.
verses.meaning: Those who do wrong are drawn to false and harmful speech — they seek it out, enjoy it, and give it authority. This principle runs both directions: wrong people produce wrong speech and also consume it gladly. What we choose to listen to reveals the state of our hearts and also shapes it further. A person who enjoys gossip, slander, and falsehood is cultivating wickedness.
verses.prayer: God, help me love truth and hate lies.
verses.discussion_question: Why do bad people love to hear lies?
verses.family_discussion: What media, conversations, or content are we allowing into our home that carries false or harmful speech? How do we guard our children's ears — and our own?
verses.do_it_today: Today, walk away or change the subject if someone starts talking badly about another person.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child covering their ears and turning away from a dark shadow whispering lies, bright light ahead, protective watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished.
verses.little_bible: If you mock a poor person, you are insulting God who made them. If you are happy when someone suffers, God will punish you.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Never mock the poor — God made them and He sees you.
verses.meaning: To mock someone who is poor is to insult their Creator, because every person is made in God's image and carries His worth. Equally, taking pleasure in another person's suffering or disaster — a form of cruel pride — will not go unpunished. God is the defender of the poor and the afflicted, and He takes personally the treatment of those made in His image.
verses.prayer: God, help me never mock those who have less.
verses.discussion_question: Why is mocking someone poor the same as insulting God?
verses.family_discussion: How do we as a family talk about people who are poor, homeless, or suffering? Are there attitudes of contempt or comparison we need to repent of and correct in front of our children?
verses.do_it_today: Look for one person today who has less than you and say or do something kind for them.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child reaching out kindly to another child in torn clothes, warm light of God's approval above them both, compassionate watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children are their fathers.
verses.little_bible: Grandchildren are the greatest gift for old people. Children find their glory in their parents. Family is a treasure.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Grandchildren are grandparents' greatest joy.
verses.meaning: Grandchildren are described as a crown — a symbol of honour and achievement — for the elderly. And children in turn derive honour and identity from their fathers. This is a verse about the beautiful mutual glory of family across generations: the old find meaning in the young, and the young stand tall in the identity given by their parents. Family is a God-given source of dignity and honour.
verses.prayer: God, thank You for my family.
verses.discussion_question: What makes your family something to be proud of?
verses.family_discussion: How are we building a legacy that our grandchildren will one day inherit — in faith, character, values, and love? What do we want them to receive from us?
verses.do_it_today: Tell a grandparent or older family member how much they mean to you today.
verses.illustration_prompt: A grandparent sitting with several grandchildren around them, all glowing with warmth and joy, a golden crown woven with love, soft watercolour family portrait

verses.kjv: Excellent speech becometh not a fool: much less do lying lips a prince.
verses.little_bible: A foolish person saying great things sounds wrong. A leader who tells lies is even worse. Words must match who you are.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A foolish person talking wisely doesn't fit. A leader who lies is even worse.
verses.meaning: There is a fundamental mismatch when a fool speaks noble words — it rings hollow and false. The contrast escalates: if a fool's fine speech is incongruous, how much more does lying become a ruler or leader? Those who hold authority are held to a higher standard of truthfulness. Character and speech must be consistent with one's position and calling.
verses.prayer: God, help my words match my heart.
verses.discussion_question: Why is lying especially wrong for a leader?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children understand that the words they speak should match who they are on the inside — that integrity means your private self and public words are the same?
verses.do_it_today: Only say things today that you really mean and that are really true.
verses.illustration_prompt: A small child in a crown whose words come out as light and truth, contrasted with a shadow figure whose words fall to the ground as broken pieces, watercolour scene

verses.kjv: A gift is as a precious stone in the eyes of him that hath it: whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth.
verses.little_bible: A gift feels like a precious gem to the one who gives it. Wherever it goes, it seems to open doors.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A gift feels precious and opens many doors.
verses.meaning: This proverb observes — with a degree of realism about human nature — that a gift (or bribe) seems almost magical to the one wielding it, opening doors and finding success wherever it goes. This is not an endorsement of bribery (which is condemned in verse 23 and elsewhere in Proverbs), but rather a clear-eyed observation that gifts carry great power in human social life, for good or ill.
verses.prayer: God, help me use gifts to bless others rightly.
verses.discussion_question: What is the difference between a gift and a bribe?
verses.family_discussion: How do we teach our children the difference between generosity (giving without expectation of return) and bribery (giving to manipulate an outcome)? Both involve gifts, but one honours God and the other corrupts justice.
verses.do_it_today: Give someone a gift today — something kind, a word, a drawing — with no strings attached.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child presenting a glowing gemstone gift with open hands, doors of light opening ahead, generous watercolour scene

verses.kjv: He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.
verses.little_bible: Forgiving a wrong done to you builds friendship. But telling everyone about it again and again destroys even best friends.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Forgiving someone builds friendship. Repeating their fault destroys it.
verses.meaning: Genuine love covers offences — it forgives rather than broadcasting the wrong. This echoes Proverbs 10:12 ('love covereth all sins') and anticipates 1 Peter 4:8. In contrast, endlessly repeating an offence — bringing it up again and again, spreading it to others — tears friendships apart, even those that seemed unbreakable. The path of love is forgiveness; the path of destruction is repetition.
verses.prayer: God, help me forgive and not repeat wrongs.
verses.discussion_question: Why does repeating someone's fault destroy friendship?
verses.family_discussion: Do we have a culture in our home of covering one another's faults in love, or do we tend to bring up past wrongs repeatedly? What would it look like to genuinely let something go?
verses.do_it_today: If someone has hurt you this week, choose today to forgive them and not bring it up again.
verses.illustration_prompt: Two children choosing to shake hands and move on, a dark cloud of past offence being covered over with warm golden light, soft watercolour scene

verses.kjv: A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool.
verses.little_bible: A wise person listens when corrected. One word of correction reaches them deeply. A foolish person learns nothing even after many beatings.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A wise person really listens when corrected. A fool doesn't learn even after many punishments.
verses.meaning: The wise person has a heart that is genuinely open to correction — a single word of rebuke penetrates and produces change. The fool, by contrast, cannot be reached even through severe physical punishment. The difference is entirely in the posture of the heart. Wisdom means being teachable; folly means being unteachable. The capacity to receive correction is itself a mark of wisdom.
verses.prayer: God, give me a heart that welcomes correction.
verses.discussion_question: What does it mean to truly listen when corrected?
verses.family_discussion: How do our children respond to correction — do they receive it, resist it, or shut down? How do we as parents model receiving correction ourselves, especially from God and from each other?
verses.do_it_today: When someone corrects you today, stop, listen, and say 'thank you' — even if it is hard.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child listening attentively to a wise elder's gentle correction, head bowed with openness, soft warm light, receptive watercolour scene

verses.kjv: An evil man seeketh only rebellion: therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him.
verses.little_bible: A wicked person only wants to cause trouble and rebel. Because of this, God will send a harsh punishment against them.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Those who keep doing wrong will face God's punishment.
verses.meaning: The evil person is characterised by a fundamental orientation toward rebellion — against authority, order, and ultimately God. This is not occasional wrongdoing but a committed pattern of defiance. The consequence is described with stark economy: a cruel messenger will be sent. God's judgment against persistent, unrepentant rebellion is certain and severe.
verses.prayer: God, keep me from a rebellious heart.
verses.discussion_question: What happens to those who keep choosing to do wrong?
verses.family_discussion: What is the difference between making a mistake, struggling with sin, and deliberately choosing rebellion? How do we help our children see the danger of a heart that sets itself against God's authority?
verses.do_it_today: If there is any area where you have been choosing to disobey God or your parents, stop today and choose the right path.
verses.illustration_prompt: A dark silhouette walking away from light into storm clouds, while a righteous child turns toward warmth and safety, contrasting watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Let a bear robbed of her whelps meet a man, rather than a fool in his folly.
verses.little_bible: A mother bear that has lost her cubs is dangerous and wild. But a foolish person doing something foolish is even more dangerous. Folly is very risky.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: An angry bear is dangerous. A fool acting foolishly is even more dangerous.
verses.meaning: A bear deprived of her cubs was proverbially one of the most dangerous animals in the ancient world (see 2 Samuel 17:8). The comparison is shocking: the proverb says that encountering such a bear is preferable to encountering a fool in the middle of their foolishness. Folly in full expression causes unpredictable, serious damage — to the fool and everyone around them. This is a warning both to avoid fools in their folly and to never become one.
verses.prayer: God, save me from foolish choices.
verses.discussion_question: Why is a fool acting foolishly so dangerous?
verses.family_discussion: Can you think of examples where someone's foolish choice caused unexpected damage to those around them? What does this teach us about why wisdom is not just a personal benefit but a gift to everyone near us?
verses.do_it_today: Before you act today, pause and ask: 'Is this wise or foolish?' Choose the wise path.
verses.illustration_prompt: A fierce mother bear in the forest, contrasted with a wild-eyed foolish figure causing chaos — a child watching from safety, cautionary watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house.
verses.little_bible: If someone does good to you and you repay them with evil, trouble will never leave your house. Evil for good brings lasting harm.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: If you do evil to someone who was good to you, trouble will stay in your home.
verses.meaning: Returning evil for good is one of the deepest betrayals in human relationships. The proverb pronounces a solemn consequence: evil shall not depart from that person's house. Their home becomes a place marked by ongoing trouble and judgment. This principle appears throughout Scripture — betrayal of benefactors brings lasting harm, while gratitude and loyalty bring blessing.
verses.prayer: God, help me always repay good with good.
verses.discussion_question: What happens when you repay someone's kindness with evil?
verses.family_discussion: Are there people in our family's life who have been good to us? How are we teaching our children to recognise, remember, and honour those relationships — and to never betray the people who have helped us?
verses.do_it_today: Think of someone who has been kind to you recently. Do or say something today to thank them.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child handing back a kind gift with gratitude, warm golden exchange, contrasted with a shadow of a house under dark clouds for those who return evil for good, watercolour scene

verses.kjv: The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with.
verses.little_bible: Starting a fight is like opening a crack in a dam. Water rushes out fast. Stop the argument before it begins.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Starting a fight is like a crack in a dam — stop it before it grows.
verses.meaning: The image of water breaking through a small opening in a dam is vivid and instructive: what begins as a tiny crack quickly becomes an unstoppable flood. Conflict works the same way — what begins as a small argument can rapidly escalate into deep and lasting division. The wise response is to stop before the first exchange, not to try to control the flood after it is released.
verses.prayer: God, help me walk away before fighting starts.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it easier to stop a fight before it starts?
verses.family_discussion: What are the common triggers in our home that open the 'crack' — the moments when a small irritation could become a flood of strife? How do we as a family agree to step back before those points?
verses.do_it_today: If you feel an argument starting today, be the first one to stop, walk away, or say something kind instead.
verses.illustration_prompt: A tiny crack in a stone dam with water beginning to trickle through, a wise child placing a hand over it to stop it, gentle watercolour scene

verses.kjv: He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.
verses.little_bible: God hates two things. Saying a guilty person is innocent. Saying an innocent person is guilty. Both are deeply wrong in His eyes.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: God hates it when people call evil good or good evil.
verses.meaning: Perverting justice in either direction — declaring the guilty innocent or the innocent guilty — is an abomination to the LORD, the strongest language of divine revulsion used in Proverbs. This verse speaks to the courts of the ancient world, but it applies universally: God is a God of perfect justice, and He is offended by any distortion of it, whether motivated by bribery, favouritism, or hatred.
verses.prayer: God, help me love what is true and right.
verses.discussion_question: Why does God hate it when justice is twisted?
verses.family_discussion: How do we teach our children that truth matters — that calling something wrong when it is right, or right when it is wrong, is not a minor social error but an offence to God who is perfectly just?
verses.do_it_today: Today, speak the truth even when it is uncomfortable. Do not call something okay when it is not.
verses.illustration_prompt: Balanced scales of justice glowing in God's light, with a child standing beside them in reverence for truth and fairness, dignified watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he hath no heart to it?
verses.little_bible: Why would a fool pay money to become wise? He does not really want wisdom in his heart. Money cannot buy a willing heart.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Money cannot buy wisdom if your heart does not want it.
verses.meaning: Wisdom cannot be purchased — it requires a willing and receptive heart. The fool has money in hand but lacks the one thing needed: genuine desire for wisdom. This proverb exposes the futility of seeking wisdom through external means while remaining inwardly closed to it. Wisdom is a matter of the heart, not of resources or opportunity.
verses.prayer: God, give me a heart that truly wants wisdom.
verses.discussion_question: Why can't money buy wisdom?
verses.family_discussion: We invest significant resources in our children's education. But is education producing wisdom — a love of truth, an openness to correction, a fear of God — or merely information? What does it mean to cultivate a child's heart toward wisdom, not just their mind?
verses.do_it_today: Ask God today for a heart that truly wants to be wise — not just to look smart, but to actually love what is good and true.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with coins in hand standing at the door of a library, but looking away with no interest, while another child runs in eagerly with empty hands, gentle watercolour scene

verses.kjv: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
verses.little_bible: A true friend loves you all the time. Not just when things are easy. A brother is made for the hard times.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A true friend loves you always, even in hard times.
verses.meaning: True friendship is not fair-weather affection — it is constant, unconditional love that persists through every season. The parallel phrase 'a brother is born for adversity' reveals the deepest purpose of close relationship: the bond between brothers (and close friends) is specifically equipped and designed for moments of hardship and suffering. The truest test of friendship is how it holds under pressure.
verses.prayer: God, help me be a faithful friend always.
verses.discussion_question: What does a real friend do when times are hard?
verses.family_discussion: Who in our family's life has been a 'born for adversity' friend — someone who showed up when things were hard? How do we raise children who will be that kind of friend to others?
verses.do_it_today: Think of a friend who might be going through something hard. Reach out to them today and let them know you are there.
verses.illustration_prompt: Two children sitting together in a rainstorm, one comforting the other, both sheltered and warm despite the storm around them, compassionate watercolour scene

verses.kjv: A man void of understanding striketh hands, and becometh surety in the presence of his friend.
verses.little_bible: A person without wisdom makes promises they cannot keep. Agreeing to pay another person's debt is very unwise.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Making promises you cannot keep shows you lack wisdom.
verses.meaning: To 'strike hands' and become surety was to pledge to repay someone else's debt if they could not. Proverbs repeatedly warns against this practice (see also 6:1–5; 11:15; 22:26–27) because it puts oneself at financial and relational risk for another's obligation. Doing this carelessly — especially for a friend, where emotional pressure is highest — marks a person as lacking good judgment.
verses.prayer: God, help me think carefully before I promise.
verses.discussion_question: Why is making promises you cannot keep unwise?
verses.family_discussion: How do we teach our children that a promise is a serious thing — that their word is their bond — and that wisdom means not making commitments beyond what we are able to keep?
verses.do_it_today: Only make one promise today — and keep it completely.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with a worried face looking at a signed agreement they cannot fulfil, a wise elder gently holding their shoulder, cautionary watercolour scene

verses.kjv: He loveth transgression that loveth strife: and he that exalteth his gate seeketh destruction.
verses.little_bible: If you love to fight, you love doing wrong. If you boast and show off too much, you are heading for destruction.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Loving to fight means loving to do wrong. Boasting leads to ruin.
verses.meaning: Loving strife and loving sin are deeply connected — conflict is not just a personality trait but a spiritual condition revealing a heart that is at war with others and with God. The second half refers to building an excessively high or grand entrance — a symbol of pride and ostentatious display — which is a path toward ruin. Both strife-seeking and pride are self-destructive.
verses.prayer: God, keep me from pride and fighting.
verses.discussion_question: Why do people who love to fight love to do wrong?
verses.family_discussion: Is there a difference between confidence and pride in our children? How do we celebrate healthy confidence while guarding against the kind of self-exaltation that sets a child on a path toward destruction?
verses.do_it_today: If you have been boasting or picking fights this week, stop and ask God to give you a humble heart instead.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with puffed-up pride standing at a tall gate that is crumbling beneath their feet, while a humble child beside them stands on solid ground, watercolour contrast scene

verses.kjv: He that hath a froward heart findeth no good: and he that hath a perverse tongue falleth into mischief.
verses.little_bible: A twisted, stubborn heart finds no good in life. A person who speaks crooked words will fall into trouble.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A stubborn wrong heart finds no good. Bad words bring trouble.
verses.meaning: 'Froward' means twisted, perverse, or stubbornly contrary. A heart oriented away from God and goodness will find no good — not because good does not exist, but because a corrupted heart cannot recognise or receive it. Equally, a perverse tongue — speech that is twisted, deceitful, or harmful — leads to mischief as a natural consequence. Inner character and outward speech are inseparably connected.
verses.prayer: God, make my heart right and my words clean.
verses.discussion_question: Why does a person with a wrong heart find no good?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children see the connection between what is in their heart and what comes out of their mouth? What practices — Scripture reading, prayer, honest conversation — help keep our hearts oriented toward God?
verses.do_it_today: Ask God to check your heart today. Ask Him: 'Is there anything in me that is twisted or wrong? Fix it, God.'
verses.illustration_prompt: A child's heart shown as a tangled knot slowly being straightened by a gentle divine hand, words of light replacing dark words, hopeful watercolour scene

verses.kjv: He that begetteth a fool doeth it to his sorrow: and the father of a fool hath no joy.
verses.little_bible: When a child grows up to be foolish, the parent carries great sorrow. A foolish child brings grief, not joy, to their parents.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A foolish child brings deep sadness to their parents.
verses.meaning: This verse is sobering for both children and parents. The parent of a fool carries a grief that does not lift — a sorrow that accompanies them. This is not meant to load guilt onto parents whose children stray despite faithful parenting, but rather to impress upon children that their choices carry real weight: the foolishness of a child is not a private matter, but a grief felt deeply by those who love them.
verses.prayer: God, help me be a joy to my parents.
verses.discussion_question: How do your choices affect the people who love you?
verses.family_discussion: How do we communicate to our children — honestly and without manipulation — that their choices bring real joy or real grief to those who love them? And how do we hold that truth alongside unconditional love?
verses.do_it_today: Do one thing today to bring joy to your parents — obey quickly, say something kind, or help without being asked.
verses.illustration_prompt: A parent's face lighting up with joy as a child makes a wise and kind choice, warm morning watercolour scene full of love and pride

verses.kjv: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
verses.little_bible: A joyful heart heals you like medicine. But a sad, crushed spirit makes you weak all the way through.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A joyful heart is like medicine for your whole body.
verses.meaning: The proverb presents a physiological and spiritual truth: the condition of the inner spirit directly affects the health of the whole person. Joy is genuinely healing — 'like a medicine' — not merely emotionally pleasant. A broken or crushed spirit, by contrast, produces a wasting effect that touches the entire person, body and soul. The inner life is not separate from the physical life.
verses.prayer: God, fill my heart with Your joy today.
verses.discussion_question: How does a joyful heart help you?
verses.family_discussion: Where does lasting joy come from — and how do we cultivate it in our home, even in difficult seasons? How do we distinguish between superficial cheerfulness and the deep joy rooted in God that Paul describes as a fruit of the Spirit?
verses.do_it_today: Find one thing to be genuinely grateful for today and tell someone about it. Let gratitude fuel your joy.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with a bright glowing heart, warmth radiating outward like healing light, a medicine bottle tipped aside as unnecessary, joyful watercolour scene

verses.kjv: A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment.
verses.little_bible: A wicked person uses secret bribes to twist justice. They pay to make wrong seem right. God hates this.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Wicked people use bribes to twist what is right and fair.
verses.meaning: The image of taking a gift 'out of the bosom' (from a hidden pocket close to the heart) suggests a secret, covert transaction — a bribe slipped quietly to corrupt the justice system. This is not a neutral observation about gift-giving (as in verse 8) but a condemnation of the deliberate use of money to pervert judgment. God who is perfectly just is deeply offended by any corruption of justice.
verses.prayer: God, help me always be honest and fair.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it wrong to pay someone to do what is unfair?
verses.family_discussion: How do we prepare our children to resist corruption in a world where bribery and dishonesty are sometimes normalised? What does it mean to have personal integrity in the face of pressure to take the easy, dishonest path?
verses.do_it_today: Be completely honest today — even in small things, even when no one is watching.
verses.illustration_prompt: A shadowy figure secretly passing a coin under a table to tip the scales of justice, while a child stands watching with a troubled, honest face, dramatic watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Wisdom is before him that hath understanding; but the eyes of a fool are in the ends of the earth.
verses.little_bible: A wise person sees wisdom right in front of them. A foolish person is always looking far away. Wisdom is here and now.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Wise people find wisdom nearby. Fools always look far away for it.
verses.meaning: The wise person has the ability to perceive wisdom close at hand — in the present moment, in Scripture, in the counsel of those around them. The fool, by contrast, is distracted — always looking to the distant horizon for something elusive, never noticing the wisdom that is present and available. Wisdom requires attentiveness to the near and the now, not a restless search for something over the horizon.
verses.prayer: God, open my eyes to wisdom around me today.
verses.discussion_question: Why does a fool always look far away for wisdom?
verses.family_discussion: Where is wisdom available to our family right now — in Scripture, in prayer, in the counsel of godly people close to us? Are we cultivating the attentiveness to notice and receive it?
verses.do_it_today: Ask a wise person near you — a parent, grandparent, or teacher — for one piece of wisdom today. Really listen.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child with eyes wide open looking at a glowing book of wisdom right in front of them, while a distracted figure stares into a blurry distant horizon, focused watercolour scene

verses.kjv: A foolish son is a grief to his father, and bitterness to her that bare him.
verses.little_bible: A foolish son makes his father deeply sad. He makes his mother feel bitter sorrow. Our choices touch our family.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A foolish child brings deep grief to both parents.
verses.meaning: The verse echoes verse 21 but adds the specific grief of the mother — 'bitterness to her that bare him.' Both parents carry the weight of a child's foolishness. The word 'bitterness' here is a strong term for deep, personal anguish. A child's choices do not exist in isolation — they ripple outward into the lives of those who love them most. This is both a warning and an invitation to choose wisdom for love's sake.
verses.prayer: God, help my life bring joy to my parents.
verses.discussion_question: How do your choices affect both your parents?
verses.family_discussion: How do we communicate — without being manipulative — the real emotional weight that a child's choices carry for their parents? And how do we make sure this is balanced with a home where children feel safe to fail, confess, and be restored?
verses.do_it_today: Think about one choice you made recently. Did it bring joy or grief to your parents? Choose better today.
verses.illustration_prompt: Two parents sitting together with bowed heads while a child's foolish decision casts a shadow over the home, then the child turning with resolve toward the light, honest watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Also to punish the just is not good, nor to strike princes for equity.
verses.little_bible: It is wrong to punish someone who has done nothing wrong. It is wrong to harm a leader just for doing what is right.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Punishing someone for doing right is always wrong.
verses.meaning: Justice requires that punishment track with guilt, not with other factors like social pressure, personal dislike, or the threat that a righteous person poses to the corrupt. To punish the innocent, or to harm a ruler for acting with equity and fairness, is a miscarriage of justice that God opposes. Righteous leaders and people must not be attacked for their righteousness.
verses.prayer: God, help me stand for what is right and fair.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it wrong to punish someone who did right?
verses.family_discussion: Have our children ever seen or experienced a situation where the right thing to do was punished or mocked? How do we prepare them for a world where righteousness sometimes comes at a cost, and help them choose it anyway?
verses.do_it_today: If you see someone being treated unfairly today, stand up for them — even if it costs you something.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child standing protectively beside another who is being falsely accused, a beam of God's approving light on the defender, courageous watercolour scene

verses.kjv: He that hath knowledge spareth his words: and a man of understanding is of an excellent spirit.
verses.little_bible: A person who truly knows things uses few words. A person of understanding has a calm and excellent spirit.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Wise people use few words and stay calm.
verses.meaning: Wisdom and self-control in speech go together. The truly knowledgeable person does not need to fill silence with words — they have learned the discipline of restraint. Alongside verbal restraint is an 'excellent spirit' — the Hebrew suggests a calm, cool, collected inner quality. Wisdom produces both verbal economy and emotional steadiness. The wise are neither verbose nor volatile.
verses.prayer: God, help me speak less and listen more.
verses.discussion_question: Why do wise people speak fewer words?
verses.family_discussion: In our home, do we honour quiet reflection and thoughtful speech, or do we reward the loudest and most talkative? How do we create space for our children to cultivate the discipline of few words and steady spirits?
verses.do_it_today: Try to speak half as many words as usual today. Think twice before you speak. Notice what changes.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child sitting quietly and thoughtfully while others around them talk loudly, a calm golden aura around the quiet child, peaceful watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding.
verses.little_bible: Even a foolish person seems wise when they stay silent. Keeping your mouth shut makes people think you understand. Silence is often the wisest answer.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Even a fool seems wise when they stay quiet.
verses.meaning: The final verse of the chapter makes the point with memorable irony: even a fool can appear wise by the simple discipline of silence. This is not an endorsement of deception, but an observation about the power of restraint — and a final sharp encouragement toward it. The inverse is equally true: much speech reveals much foolishness. The discipline of silence is available to everyone, even before wisdom is fully formed.
verses.prayer: God, help me know when to be quiet.
verses.discussion_question: Why does staying quiet sometimes show wisdom?
verses.family_discussion: How do we distinguish between wise silence (restraint, thoughtfulness, listening) and unhelpful silence (avoidance, passivity, hiding)? How do we model each for our children?
verses.do_it_today: The next time you feel the urge to say something unnecessary, hold your peace. Let God fill the silence.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child sitting with lips gently closed amid a noisy group, a small crown of wisdom softly resting on their head, peaceful and thoughtful watercolour scene
